subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain at the moment of attachment on day twelve with a wedge shaped nipple after feeds
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman twelve days after the birth of her first baby. She has come because feeding has become so painful that she has been dreading each feed and has started giving one bottle of formula overnight.

She describes a sharp stabbing pain at the instant the baby latches on that eases considerably once the milk starts flowing, and that has gone by the time the feed ends. There is no burning between feeds and no shooting pain into the breast afterwards. On examination both nipples have a linear crack at the base and, immediately after she takes the baby off, the nipple comes out compressed into a wedge with a white crease across the tip. The areolae are not red or shiny and there is no scaling. The baby's mouth is clear with no white plaques, and he has regained his birth weight and is having six heavy nappies a day.

data_table.Examination: Linear fissure at the base of each nipple, nipple compressed into a wedge shape with a transverse white crease immediately after the feed, areolae not erythematous or shiny, no scaling or satellite lesions, breasts soft with no localised lump or erythema
data_table.Infant: Birth weight regained by day twelve, six heavy nappies daily, oral cavity clear with no plaques, tongue elevates to the palate with the mouth open

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Observe a full feed and correct attachment with lactation support
options.rationale: Pain confined to the moment of attachment with a nipple that emerges compressed and creased indicates that the nipple is being drawn against the hard palate rather than deep to the junction with the soft palate, which is a positioning problem and the cause of the fissures. Watching an entire feed is the only way to identify and correct it, and the fissures heal once the mechanical cause is removed (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe topical miconazole for her nipples and oral gel for the baby
options.rationale: Nipple candidiasis causes burning pain that persists between feeds and often radiates into the breast, with shiny or flaking areolae and usually oral plaques in the baby, and none of those features is present. Treating for the wrong cause leaves the mechanical trauma to continue (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe oral fluconazole for her and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Systemic antifungal treatment is reserved for deep breast pain thought to be candidal that has not responded to topical treatment, and it differs from the topical option only in the depth of the infection it targets. Neither applies to pain that stops when the feed does (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Advise nipple shields for every feed and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: A shield can be a short term measure while damaged nipples heal, but used without correcting the attachment it perpetuates the shallow latch, and it is associated with reduced milk transfer and earlier weaning. It manages the symptom while entrenching the cause (Source: Australian Breastfeeding Association: Nipple pain).

options.text: Prescribe topical mupirocin to the cracks and continue feeding as she is
options.rationale: Topical antibiotic is appropriate when a fissure shows honey coloured crusting, spreading erythema or purulent discharge suggesting secondary bacterial infection, none of which is described here. Continuing to feed unchanged also guarantees the fissures reopen at every feed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Nipple pain is the commonest reason Australian women stop breastfeeding earlier than they intended, and the great majority of it is mechanical rather than infective. The timing of the pain is the most useful piece of history: pain at attachment that eases as the feed progresses points to a shallow latch, whereas burning that persists between feeds with radiating breast pain suggests candidal infection, and pain with blanching then colour change of the nipple after feeds suggests vasospasm. A nipple that emerges compressed, creased or wedge shaped is direct evidence of compression against the hard palate. Assessment requires observing a complete feed rather than examining the nipple alone, and correction focuses on bringing the baby to the breast chin first with a wide gape so the nipple sits deep in the mouth. Persistent difficulty despite skilled support prompts assessment for tongue tie, but the great majority resolve with positioning alone.
key_points: The timing of nipple pain relative to the feed identifies the cause
Pain only at attachment with a compressed creased nipple indicates a shallow latch
Candidal pain burns between feeds and usually involves shiny or flaking areolae
Observing a full feed is essential and cannot be replaced by examining the nipple
Nipple shields without attachment correction perpetuate the problem
explanation.pearls: Look at the shape of the nipple in the first seconds after the baby comes off the breast, because a nipple that is round and everted has been positioned correctly while one shaped like a new lipstick has been compressed against the hard palate throughout the feed.

subtopic_detail: Three days of headache and nausea that improve at work in a couple using an unflued gas heater, with normal oxygen saturation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old man brought in by ambulance on a cold July morning. He has had three days of headache, nausea and difficulty concentrating that are worst in the evenings at home and that he had noticed clear up during his shifts at work.

His partner called the ambulance because she found him slumped in a chair this morning and could not rouse him for what she estimates was about half a minute before he came round confused. She has had similar headaches over the same three days and is eighteen weeks pregnant. They have been running an old unflued gas heater in the lounge room continuously because of the cold. On arrival he is alert but slow to answer, his skin is a normal colour, his chest is clear and there are no focal neurological signs. His oxygen saturation reads 99 per cent on room air and his arterial blood gas shows a normal partial pressure of oxygen with a carboxyhaemoglobin of 22 per cent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Carboxyhaemoglobin 22 per cent (less than 3 in non smokers), arterial partial pressure of oxygen 96 mmHg (80-100), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), troponin within normal limits, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic change
data_table.Examination: Alert but slowed responses, normal skin colour, clear chest, no focal neurological deficit, no cherry red discolouration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for him?

options.text: Give oxygen by nasal prongs at 4 L per minute and observe him for six hours
options.rationale: Low flow oxygen delivers a fraction of inspired oxygen well below what is needed, and the elimination half life of the toxin falls from around five hours on room air to about ninety minutes only when the inspired concentration approaches 100 per cent. Underdosing oxygen is the commonest error in this poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give high flow oxygen and discharge him once his symptoms have settled
options.rationale: High flow oxygen is correct but discharge on symptom resolution ignores the delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome, which follows in up to 40 per cent of significant exposures days to weeks later, and it returns him to an uncorrected source. Symptomatic improvement is not the endpoint of care (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Arrange a CT of his brain before starting any specific treatment for him
options.rationale: Imaging delays the only treatment that removes the toxin and would be normal early in the illness, since the basal ganglia changes described in this poisoning appear late. Oxygen is started immediately and imaging reserved for focal signs or failure to improve (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 94 per cent and admit him for observation
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish the abnormal haemoglobin species from oxyhaemoglobin, so the reading of 99 per cent is falsely reassuring and titrating to it would deliver almost no oxygen. This poisoning is one of the specific exceptions to conservative oxygen targets (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give high flow oxygen and refer him urgently for hyperbaric treatment
options.rationale: Loss of consciousness at any point, along with a carboxyhaemoglobin above 25 per cent, neurological signs, myocardial ischaemia or pregnancy, are the accepted indications for hyperbaric therapy, and his witnessed unresponsiveness meets that bar even at 22 per cent. High flow oxygen through a tight fitting reservoir mask is started immediately while the referral is being made (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with an affinity around 240 times that of oxygen, shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left and binds cytochrome oxidase, so tissue hypoxia occurs despite a normal arterial partial pressure of oxygen. Standard pulse oximeters read the abnormal species as oxyhaemoglobin and therefore report a normal saturation, which is why the diagnosis depends on a co oximetry measurement on a blood gas and on the epidemiology of the story. The pattern of multiple people in one household with headache, nausea and confusion that improves on leaving the building, in winter, with an unflued heater or a generator, is the recognisable presentation. Treatment is high flow oxygen through a reservoir mask, continued until symptoms resolve and the level normalises, with hyperbaric oxygen considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac ischaemia, a level above 25 per cent or pregnancy. Foetal haemoglobin binds the toxin more avidly than adult haemoglobin, so a pregnant contact needs assessment and treatment on lower thresholds regardless of how well she feels.
key_points: Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin and is falsely normal
Diagnosis requires co oximetry, prompted by the household and seasonal pattern
High flow oxygen by reservoir mask shortens the half life from about five hours to ninety minutes
Loss of consciousness, neurological signs, ischaemia, a level above 25 per cent or pregnancy prompt hyperbaric referral
Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae occur days to weeks later and require follow up
explanation.pearls: Assess and treat every person and pet from the same household even when they feel well, and arrange for the source to be inspected before anyone returns, because the second presentation from the same address is usually more severe than the first.

sources.label: Australian Resuscitation Council: Hypoxia and poisoning

subtopic_detail: Reduced libido and delayed ejaculation five months into successful treatment in a man whose earlier dose reduction caused relapse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 34 year old man who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for eight months for a first episode of major depression. His mood has been well for five months, he has returned to full time work and to playing football, and he no longer wakes early or ruminates.

Since about the third week of treatment he has had markedly reduced sexual interest and takes a very long time to reach orgasm, which is causing tension with his partner. He tells you he still wakes with normal erections and can maintain an erection without difficulty. Six weeks ago the dose was reduced to 50 mg daily to see whether it would help, and within a fortnight his early morning waking and low mood returned, so the dose was put back to 100 mg and his mood recovered. He drinks two standard drinks a week, takes no other medication and uses no recreational drugs. His testosterone, thyroid function and fasting glucose are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, normal secondary sexual characteristics, no gynaecomastia, body mass index 25 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Morning total testosterone, thyroid stimulating hormone, prolactin, fasting glucose and lipid profile all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily for eight months, no other prescribed or over the counter medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Stop the sertraline now given that his depression is in remission
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment is continued for at least six to twelve months after remission of a first episode to prevent relapse, and this man has already relapsed once on dose reduction at five months. Ceasing entirely would trade a side effect for a recurrence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch him to an antidepressant with a lower rate of sexual side effects
options.rationale: Sexual dysfunction from serotonin reuptake inhibition affects up to half of patients, rarely improves with time and is dose related, and his relapse on dose reduction has already closed off the simplest alternative. Agents such as agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide and vortioxetine carry substantially lower rates and allow effective treatment to continue (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add sildenafil as required before sexual activity and continue the sertraline
options.rationale: A phosphodiesterase inhibitor helps erectile dysfunction, and his erections are normal on waking and during activity, so the problem lies with desire and orgasm rather than with tumescence. It targets a mechanism that is not the one affected here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose and review his mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable first strategy in general, but it has already been tried at exactly this dose and produced return of early morning waking and low mood within a fortnight. Repeating a failed intervention risks a second relapse (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure him the effect will resolve with time and make no change now
options.rationale: Tolerance to sexual adverse effects develops in only a minority and his symptoms have persisted for eight months, so waiting is not supported. Unaddressed sexual dysfunction is also one of the leading reasons patients stop antidepressants without telling their doctor (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Sexual dysfunction is among the most common and most under reported adverse effects of serotonergic antidepressants, affecting between 25 and 70 per cent of patients depending on how it is measured, and it involves desire, arousal and orgasm to differing degrees. Distinguishing it from the sexual dysfunction of depression itself is done on timing, since drug related effects begin within the first weeks of treatment or a dose increase while depressive dysfunction improves as mood improves. Management options are watchful waiting, dose reduction, a drug holiday, switching to a lower risk agent, or augmentation, and the choice depends on how stable the mood is and what has already been tried. Paroxetine has the highest reported rates and agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide, bupropion and vortioxetine the lowest. Any switch is made with attention to discontinuation symptoms and to the risk of relapse during the changeover, usually by cross tapering rather than abrupt substitution.
key_points: Sexual dysfunction affects a large minority to a majority of patients on serotonergic antidepressants
Onset within weeks of starting or increasing the dose distinguishes it from depressive dysfunction
Tolerance develops in only a minority so waiting is rarely the answer
Relapse on a previous dose reduction removes that option from the list
Agomelatine, mirtazapine, moclobemide and vortioxetine carry the lowest rates
explanation.pearls: Ask about sexual function before starting an antidepressant and again at the four week review, because a baseline recorded before treatment is the only way to separate a drug effect from the sexual dysfunction that depression itself causes in around 40 per cent of patients.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler drinking over a litre of cow's milk daily with a ferritin of 6
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 22 month old boy referred because he looks pale and has become increasingly irritable and tired over the past three months. His parents say he has stopped wanting to walk far and asks to be carried.

He still takes a bottle of cow's milk to bed and drinks roughly 1.2 litres a day, and his parents describe him as refusing almost all meat, vegetables and cereals in favour of milk and yoghurt. His stools are normal in colour and consistency with no blood, and he has had no vomiting, fevers or overseas travel. He was born at term to a mother whose own iron levels were normal, and he has no family history of anaemia or of blood disorders. On examination he is pale with pale conjunctivae, has a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and has no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, bruising or petechiae. His height and weight are both on the 25th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 62 fL (73-85), red cell distribution width 19 per cent (11.5-14.5), platelets 486 x10^9/L (150-450), ferritin 6 mcg/L (15-150), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, coeliac serology negative with normal total immunoglobulin A
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae and skin, soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, no bruising or petechiae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count afterwards
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, cardiac failure or a haemoglobin below about 60 to 70 g/L with symptoms, and a child who is walking about with a compensated chronic anaemia does not qualify. Transfusing also carries the risk of circulatory overload in slowly developed anaemia (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron infusion as a single dose day procedure
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is reserved for children who cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron, or who have ongoing losses outpacing replacement, and it requires a day procedure with a small risk of hypersensitivity. Nothing here suggests oral therapy will fail (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Thalassaemia trait shares microcytosis with this picture but is distinguished by a normal or high ferritin, a normal red cell distribution width and a red cell count that is high for the haemoglobin. A ferritin of 6 mcg/L with a normal C reactive protein already establishes iron deficiency, and electrophoresis performed while iron deplete can also falsely lower the haemoglobin A2 fraction (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Start oral iron and reduce his cow's milk to under 500 mL a day
options.rationale: Excessive cow's milk is the classic Australian cause in this age group, displacing iron rich foods, providing calcium and casein that inhibit iron absorption, and causing occult gut blood loss, so replacement fails unless the intake is capped. Oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily with dietary change corrects the deficiency and is continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises to refill stores (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

options.text: Refer him for upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy to find blood loss
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated when there is overt bleeding, growth failure, gastrointestinal symptoms or failure to respond to adequate oral iron, and he has normal stools, normal growth and negative coeliac serology. An anaesthetic and endoscopy before a trial of treatment inverts the sequence (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency in Australian toddlers and excessive cow's milk intake is its leading cause, through three separate mechanisms: displacement of iron rich foods, inhibition of absorption by calcium and casein, and occult intestinal blood loss from a milk induced enteropathy. The recommendation is to cap cow's milk at about 500 mL per day from twelve months and to avoid bottles at bedtime. The blood picture is a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a raised red cell distribution width, often a reactive thrombocytosis, and a low ferritin, though ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant so a concurrent C reactive protein is needed to interpret it. Differentials are thalassaemia trait, which has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width, lead exposure, and coeliac disease. Treatment is oral elemental iron at 3 to 6 mg per kilogram daily continued for three months after the haemoglobin normalises, and failure to respond within a month usually means poor adherence, continued milk intake or an unrecognised cause of loss.
key_points: Cow's milk above about 500 mL a day is the leading cause in Australian toddlers
A low ferritin with a normal C reactive protein confirms iron deficiency
Thalassaemia trait has a normal ferritin and a normal red cell distribution width
Oral iron continues for three months after the haemoglobin normalises
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or cardiac failure
explanation.pearls: Expect the reticulocyte count to rise within three to five days and the haemoglobin to climb by around 10 g/L per fortnight, so a repeat count at four weeks that has not moved points to adherence, ongoing milk intake or the wrong diagnosis rather than to a need for a higher dose.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Children's dosing companion

subtopic_detail: Worsening wheeze at 28 weeks in a woman who stopped her inhaled preventer early in pregnancy, speaking in short phrases
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 27 year old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy with two days of worsening wheeze and breathlessness following a head cold.

She has had asthma since childhood and was well controlled on budesonide with formoterol before conceiving, but she stopped the preventer at eight weeks because she was worried about the effect on the baby and has been using salbutamol alone, most recently every three to four hours. She is sitting upright and can speak only in short phrases, using her accessory muscles. Her chest has widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry at both bases. Her peak expiratory flow is 210 L/min against a recorded personal best of 470 L/min. Her oxygen saturation is 93 per cent on room air, her respiratory rate is 28 per minute and the cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 155 per minute with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, foetal heart rate 155 per minute
data_table.Investigations: Peak expiratory flow 210 L/min against a personal best of 470 L/min, arterial pH 7.46 with partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mmHg (pregnancy reference 28-32), no consolidation on chest radiograph with abdominal shielding
data_table.Examination: Speaking in short phrases, accessory muscle use, widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced basal air entry, cardiotocograph with normal baseline variability and accelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol alone and avoid systemic corticosteroid in pregnancy
options.rationale: Withholding systemic corticosteroid is the central error in this scenario, since prednisolone is extensively metabolised by placental 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase so that foetal exposure is a small fraction of the maternal dose. Maternal hypoxia poses a far greater risk to the foetus than the drug (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate as the first treatment for her wheeze
options.rationale: Magnesium is an adjunct for severe or life threatening exacerbations that have not responded to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid treatment, not a first line agent. Using it first delays the interventions with the largest and fastest effect (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

options.text: Give oxygen with repeated salbutamol and start systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated exactly as it is outside pregnancy, with oxygen targeted to a saturation of 94 to 98 per cent, repeated or continuous inhaled salbutamol with ipratropium for severe episodes, and systemic corticosteroid given early. Her inability to complete sentences with a peak flow at 45 per cent of personal best places her in the severe category where the corticosteroid is the intervention that changes the trajectory (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange urgent delivery of the baby to relieve her respiratory distress
options.rationale: Birth at 28 weeks carries substantial prematurity risk and does not treat bronchoconstriction, and the cardiotocograph here is reassuring. Delivery is considered only for a deteriorating mother requiring ventilation or for foetal compromise that persists despite maternal treatment (Source: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy).
source_refs: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy

options.text: Give nebulised adrenaline and observe her for the next four hours
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is used for upper airway obstruction such as croup or angio oedema rather than for lower airway bronchospasm, where a selective beta2 agonist is both more effective and better tolerated. Four hours of observation without corticosteroid also wastes the window in which it acts (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of women with asthma worsen during pregnancy, and the strongest predictor of an exacerbation is stopping the preventer, which around a quarter of pregnant women do out of concern about the medication. Poorly controlled asthma is associated with pre-eclampsia, foetal growth restriction, preterm birth and low birth weight, whereas the inhaled and systemic drugs used to treat it have reassuring safety records. Acute management is identical to the non pregnant algorithm, with the additional points that maternal oxygen saturation is kept at or above 94 per cent because the foetus sits on the steep part of its own dissociation curve, and that the woman is nursed with left lateral tilt after twenty weeks. Physiological hyperventilation of pregnancy means the normal partial pressure of carbon dioxide is around 28 to 32 mmHg, so a value in the normal non pregnant range signals impending failure. Continuous foetal monitoring is used in severe episodes, and every discharge includes restarting the preventer with a written action plan.
key_points: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated the same as outside pregnancy
Systemic corticosteroid is given early and is not withheld because of pregnancy
Target maternal oxygen saturation at or above 94 per cent to protect foetal oxygenation
A partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the normal non pregnant range signals deterioration
Preventer cessation is the leading cause of exacerbation in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Take the peak flow as a percentage of the woman's own personal best rather than a predicted value, since peak expiratory flow itself is essentially unchanged by pregnancy and a reading below 50 per cent of personal best defines a severe exacerbation at any gestation.

sources.label: National Asthma Council Australia: Asthma in pregnancy
